item.title: “One who has cut off craving, Without remainder, Dried up the swift stream — That monk abandons the near and far shore, Like a serpent…
item.description:
“One who has cut off craving,
Without remainder,
Dried up the swift stream —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

“One who has destroyed conceit,
Without remainder,
As a great flood destroys a fragile reed —
That monk abandons the near and far shore,
Like a serpent sheds its worn-out skin.”

From: Sutta Nipāta 1.1

item.title: “Monks, there are these three elements of escape. What three? The escape from sensual pleasures — that is renunciation. The escape from form — that…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these three elements of escape. What three? The escape from sensual pleasures — that is renunciation. The escape from form — that is the formless. And as to whatever has come to be, is conditioned, dependently arisen, its escape is its cessation. These, monks, are the three elements of escape.

Knowing the escape from sensual pleasures,
And transcending all forms,
Always ardent, calming all conditioned things —
That monk sees rightly.

From that, being thus liberated,
He perfects direct knowledge,
Dwells at peace, in that very life,
That sage has crossed beyond all yokes.”

From: Itivuttaka 72

item.title: “Monks, just as a defiled, dusty cloth, if placed in clean water becomes clean, if placed in a furnace becomes clean. So too, monks, a…
item.description:
“Monks, just as a defiled, dusty cloth, if placed in clean water becomes clean, if placed in a furnace becomes clean. So too, monks, a monk of such virtue, such quality, such wisdom – even if he eats almsfood of choice rice with black grains removed, various soups and curries – that does not become an obstacle for him.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 7 – Vatthūpamasutta

item.title: “Monks, for direct knowledge of craving, ten things should be developed. What ten? The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of disgust…
item.description:
“Monks, for direct knowledge of craving, ten things should be developed. What ten? The perception of foulness, the perception of death, the perception of disgust with food, the perception of non-delight in the entire world, the perception of impermanence, the perception of suffering in impermanence, the perception of not-self in suffering, the perception of abandoning, the perception of dispassion, the perception of cessation. For direct knowledge of craving, monks, these ten things should be developed.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.237

item.title: … (At Sāvatthi). Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: As if struck by a sword,…
item.description:
… (At Sāvatthi). Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
As if struck by a sword,
As if fire blazed on the head —
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning lust for sensual pleasures.

(The Blessed One):
As if struck by a sword,
As if fire blazed on the head —
Mindful, a monk should go forth,
Abandoning identity view.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.21

item.title: “Cunda, just as all unwholesome states tend downward and all wholesome states tend upward. So too, Cunda: the harmless person is higher than the harmful…
item.description:
“Cunda, just as all unwholesome states tend downward and all wholesome states tend upward. So too, Cunda: the harmless person is higher than the harmful person; the person who abstains from killing is higher than the killer; the person who abstains from taking what is not given is higher than the taker of what is not given; the person unsmeared by the world, not clinging to personal views, of easy disposition and equanimity, is higher than the person smeared by the world, clinging to personal views, of difficult disposition and lacking equanimity.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 8 – Sallekhasutta

item.title: Elder Sabbhakāma: This two-footed creature, Impure and foul-smelling, Full of various corpses — From it, fluid oozes. With deer, use a trap; with fish, a…
item.description:
Elder Sabbhakāma:

This two-footed creature,
Impure and foul-smelling,
Full of various corpses —
From it, fluid oozes.

With deer, use a trap; with fish, a hook;
With monkeys, a pit;
Thus worldlings are caught.

Forms, sounds, tastes, smells, touches —
Agreeable and pleasing —
These five strands of sensual pleasure
Are known in female form.

Worldlings, with mind infatuated,
Run after enjoying female form.
The terrifying cemetery increases,
Storing up renewed existence.

One who avoids female form
As a foot avoids a snake’s head —
That mindful one overcomes
The world’s poisoner.

Seeing the danger in sensual pleasures,
Security in renunciation,
Having escaped all sensual pleasures,
I have attained the destruction of defilements.

From: Theragāthā 6.14

item.title: “Monks, these six sense bases — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness. What six? The eye sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained…
item.description:
“Monks, these six sense bases — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness. What six? The eye sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — brings happiness. The ear … The nose … The tongue … The body … The mind sense base, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — brings happiness. These six sense bases, monks — well-guarded, well-protected, well-guarded, well-restrained — bring happiness.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 35.94

item.title: … Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One: Life is swept along, Short is the lifespan…
item.description:
… Standing to one side, that deity recited this verse in the presence of the Blessed One:
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Do meritorious deeds
That bring true happiness.

(The Blessed One):
Life is swept along,
Short is the lifespan —
To old age we are led,
There is no stopping place.
Seeing this danger in death,
Seeking peace, abandon worldly hopes.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 1.3

item.title: “Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s…
item.description:
“Monks, ‘bait’ is a synonym for the five strands of sensual pleasure. ‘Hunter’ is a synonym for Māra. ‘Hunter’s followers’ are a synonym for Māra’s followers. ‘Herd of deer’ is a synonym for ascetics and brahmins. Here, monks, the first kind of ascetics and brahmins, entering and indulging, eat the bait cast by Māra and the world’s offerings. Having entered and indulged, they eat those foods, become infatuated; from infatuation, they become heedless; from heedlessness, they become subject to Māra’s will among that bait and those offerings. Thus, monks, these first ascetics and brahmins have not escaped Māra’s power.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 25 – Nivāpasutta
